data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001 argues that sky view factor is the 'single dominant cross-city modulator' of nocturnal UHI magnitude, but it conflates SVF's radiative-trapping role with the stored-thermal-mass effect it is supposed to be modulating. The mechanism text says low SVF 'slows the nocturnal cooling rate, so the stored thermal mass effect persists longer' — i.e., SVF's influence is mediated through how long stored heat persists, not through the amount of heat stored or released. On a clear, calm night the heat island is driven by the absolute release of stored sensible heat, which depends on thermal admittance and building materials; if one city has much higher thermal mass (and thus releases more stored heat) but only moderately higher SVF, SVF-based radiative trapping cannot account for the larger gap. The target's own counterconditions concede this: it offers no principled reason why thermal mass differences across cities are always subordinate to SVF differences, yet it asserts SVF as the single best modulator. For the specific problem — which asks for the single mechanism best explaining why the night-time gap is larger in some cities than in others — the target over-privileges a geometry variable without establishing that radiative trapping dominates over heat-storage capacity as a cross-city control.
